bodies: ee The number of commodities now moving in the trade between Europe and the Far East numbers several hundred items for which individual rates have to be established to meet shipper’s requirements. In contrast to earlier times with a limited number of commodities, ports of call and members, it is not surprising why the functioning of a Conference is no longer as easy to regulate. Besides changes in economical, commercial and technological factors, the Far Eastern Freight Conference itself has undergone changes in composition

Following discussions with the Singapore National Shippers’ Council (SNSC), Lines of the FEFC have agreed to a trial operation which began earlier in March for spot physical cargo control checks in Singapore. In other FEFC areas where there has been found to be a need for it, cargo control is already operative and in Singapore, spot checks at destination are already being conducted on Eastbound cargoes loaded in Europe. These physical checks are in addition to documentary control and the Lines reserve the right, under the bill of lading, to do spot physical checks on out-turn of Singapore cargoes at European destinations too. In its explanation for the introduction of an iterium scheme of physical checks, the FEFC stated that Singapore was the obvious place to carry them out in order to effect a full-scale operation. This was revealed by Mr. W.J. Cook, FEFC Representative for Malaysia and Singapore who also added that if it had not been proven necessary, the FEFC would not commit itself to this move. . The essential reasons for steps taken by the Conference are principally to ensure uniformity in application of tariff rates and conditions from Line to Line, and more importantly, from shipper to shipper. This will eliminate agents of Lines from demanding any more freight than the tariff already specified from shippers. The new exercise in Singapore covers those commodities which are not already subject to special measuring and these include rubber, which is already checked under the rubber rules in the tariff, while timber is shipped under special arrangements.

Representative of the German company in Singapore, Mr. Lutz Schuessler describes this attachment that will ensure speed and considerable savings in manpower and operation costs. When fitted an O & KL6 wheel loader, it can handle and plant sapling trees using hydraulically-operated cage and spades and is capable of uprooting a tree of up to 160 cm in circumference within a minute. The wheel loader on the other hand is a popular equipment in the construction and building industries and in other areas where there is a need for a compact loading unit. It has no clutch or gears and reverse of the hydrostatic drive can simply be operated by the foot pedal. The O & K L6 wheel loader is powered by a Deutz 43—horsepower air-cooled diesel engine and is capable of a top speed of 20 km/hr.

A S$3 million electrical equipment contract for the world’s biggest offshore tin dredger now being built in Singapore has been won by West Germany‘s AEG-—Telefunken, represented here and in Malaysia by the Behn Meyer Group. The Complete electrical equipment of the dredger supplied by AEG—Telefunken will include: six three-phase AC generators with 6,200 KVa total output plus the associated switchboards; seven thyristorfed, speed-controlled DC motors with a total output of 3,400 kw, together with all necessary switching and controlling devices; the drives for the additional control and auxiliary winches as well as for the pumps, The complete system of the 110-metre long bucket-chain dredger will be controlled and monitored from a central operator's console. Providing technical and manpower backup for the installation of the equipment where necessary will be Behn Meyer’s special Marine Electrical Equipment Division which was closely involved in the negotiations of the contract. The dredger, presently being constructed by Jurong Shipbuilders Pte. Ltd., is expected to be delivered to Indonesia in 1978.

The secret of efficiency is to choose the correct type of pumping unit with the correct flow and velocity relationship to suit the size and speed of the craft to be propelled. This unit is driven by a marinised conventional engine of suitable horsepower for the desired performance. The Hamilton system is the result of lengthy experiments and many years of development. It has high efficiency, excellent manoeuvrability and a host of impressive advantages over the conventional propeller: It has a very shallow draft with nothing extending below the bottom — no skeg, rudder, shaft, propeller. Obviously this is very desirable when running in shallow water or near underwater obstructions that could ruin a prop or wipe-off a rudder in short order. Simplicity of installation is another important factor. The jet drive eliminates the need of gearboxes, reversing clutches and V-drives, since the pump itself, mounted above the bottom line, drives directly from the engine. For reversing, there is no need for a gearbox because the impeller continues to rotate alwsays the same direction. To slow, stop or reverse the boat, a mechanical deflector is manually activated over the jet.stream diverting it in the opposite direction. This causes a reverse thrust and consequent opposite action to the boat’s direction and motion. Steering is obtained by a pair of deflector plates arranged one either side of the nozzle. They are suitably connected by linkage and cables to the steering wheel. A powerful steering action results from turning the complete jet stream left or right.
